metadata.title: Studying the comparability of student perceptions of teaching quality across 38 countries
metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 student questionnaire responses from 38 countries (excluding Singapore) and applies TIMSS sampling weights to support representativeness and cross-country comparability. For analyses conducted on single-country samples, the authors used the total student weight (TOTWGT) to ensure the sample represents the national population. For analyses combining multiple countries, they used the senate weight (SENWGT), which standardizes country contribution by summing to the same size across countries so that each country is treated as an equal contributor regardless of its sample size. To account for the nested structure of students within classrooms, they adjusted standard errors and model fit by using TYPE=COMPLEX in Mplus.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not predict cognitive achievement scores with Plausible Values; instead, it evaluates measurement invariance and comparability of latent constructs from student questionnaire items (behavioral management and instructional clarity). Because the dependent variables are questionnaire-based latent factors rather than PV-based achievement outcomes, PV handling is not applicable. For missing data, the authors explicitly state that item-level missingness (2.3%–8.9%) was handled with Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML), which corresponds to multiple-imputation-style likelihood-based handling in this schema.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 assessment data were used across 39 participating countries, but Singapore was excluded because it did not include the behavioral management scale in the student questionnaire. The analytic dataset therefore consists of nationally representative responses from Grade 8 students (and their mathematics teachers) from 38 countries. The study uses the two teaching-quality constructs measured in the TIMSS 2019 student questionnaire: behavioral management (six items) and instructional clarity (seven items, with one item excluded from the original scale due to different pronoun reference). Missing item responses in the total sample ranged from 2.3% to 8.9% and were handled with Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML).

The authors first fit a two-factor measurement model and evaluate exact measurement invariance using multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (configural, then metric, then scalar), reporting fit indices such as CFI/TLI/RMSEA/SRMR. Metric invariance was supported (ΔCFI=0.007; ΔRMSEA=0.002), but scalar invariance was not (ΔCFI=0.036; ΔRMSEA=0.015), implying that mean comparisons across countries are not justified under exact invariance. They then applied the alignment method for approximate invariance and used Monte Carlo simulation to assess reliability of factor-mean/variance recovery. Despite improved interpretability for instructional clarity, the alignment method did not substantially increase comparability for mean-score use; the authors caution that TIMSS international mean scores may be misleading for substantive cross-country interpretation. data.outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 student questionnaire data to assess cross-national comparability of two latent teaching-quality constructs—behavioral management and instructional clarity—across 38 countries (Singapore excluded). The authors first fit a two-factor measurement model and evaluate exact measurement invariance using multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (configural, then metric, then scalar), reporting fit indices such as CFI/TLI/RMSEA/SRMR. Metric invariance was supported (ΔCFI=0.007; ΔRMSEA=0.002), but scalar invariance was not (ΔCFI=0.036; ΔRMSEA=0.015), implying that mean comparisons across countries are not justified under exact invariance. They then applied the alignment method for approximate invariance and used Monte Carlo simulation to assess reliability of factor-mean/variance recovery. Despite improved interpretability for instructional clarity, the alignment method did not substantially increase comparability for mean-score use; the authors caution that TIMSS international mean scores may be misleading for substantive cross-country interpretation.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This paper is a measurement-invariance and comparability study using multi-group CFA and the alignment optimization method, not a predictive ML modeling study. As a result, there are no ML algorithms, no PV-based achievement targets, and no supervised predictive performance metrics to extract into main_findings. The main empirical outputs are measurement-model fit indices (CFI/TLI/RMSEA/SRMR), invariance decision thresholds (ΔCFI/ΔRMSEA), and alignment non-invariance summaries (non-invariant parameter percentages and R-square values), which are outside the ML-target schema.
